title: Problem Overview (DISPROVED)
content:
**Erdos Problem #34** asked: For a permutation pi, is S(pi) = o(n^2)?

S(pi) counts distinct consecutive sums: sums of the form sum_{i=u}^v pi(i).

**Answer**: NO! The conjecture is FALSE.

**History**:
- Identity permutation: S(iota) = o(n^2) (motivated the conjecture)
- Hegyvari (1986): First counterexample with S(pi) >= (1/18)n^2
- Konieczny (2015): S(pi) >= n^2/4 is achievable

The conjecture is 'extremely false'!
mathContext: A permutation pi in S_n rearranges {1,...,n}. Consecutive sums are contiguous subsequence sums.

title: Consecutive Sum
content:
**consecutiveSum n pi u v** computes the sum of pi(i) for i from u to v.

If u <= v, this is sum_{i in [u,v]} (pi(i) + 1), where +1 converts from 0-indexed Fin n to 1-indexed values.

If u > v, the sum is 0 (empty range).
mathContext: For the identity, consecutive sums are arithmetic progressions: (v-u+1)(u+v+2)/2.
prerequisites: summation over an interval of indices

title: S(pi) - Count of Distinct Sums
content:
**S n pi** is the cardinality of all distinct consecutive sums.

This is the main quantity studied. For random pi, S(pi) ~ 0.284n^2.

For the identity, S(iota) = O(n^1.5) = o(n^2), which is much smaller.
prerequisites: cardinality of a set of distinct values
consecutive sums over index pairs u <= v
asymptotic growth rates n^1.5 versus n^2

title: The Disproved Conjecture
content:
**ErdosConjecture** states: For all epsilon > 0, there exists N such that for all n > N and all pi in S_n, S(pi) < epsilon * n^2.

This is FALSE, as documented in the file's comments: counterexamples exist with S(pi) >= cn^2 for constant c > 0 (specifically c >= 1/4). NOTE: the falsity of ErdosConjecture is not formalized as a Lean declaration in this file -- it is recorded only in prose comments.
mathContext: The little-o notation S(pi) = o(n^2) means S(pi)/n^2 -> 0 as n -> infinity.
prerequisites: negation of a universally quantified statement

title: Hegyvari's Counterexample (1986)
content:
A comment documents that there exist permutations with S(pi) >= (1/18 + o(1))n^2 (Hegyvari, 1986).

This was the FIRST counterexample to Erdos's conjecture.

1/18 ~ 0.056 shows the conjecture fails by a constant factor. NOTE: this bound is not formalized as a Lean declaration -- it is documentation only.
mathContext: Hegyvari's construction is explicit but the 1/18 constant was later improved dramatically.
prerequisites: quadratic lower bound with o(1) error term

title: Konieczny's Quarter Bound (2015)
content:
A comment documents that there exist permutations with S(pi) >= n^2/4 (Konieczny, 2015).

This shows the conjecture is 'extremely false' - not just failing by a small constant, but by a factor of 1/4.

Since max possible is ~n^2/2 pairs, this is nearly half the theoretical maximum! NOTE: this bound is not formalized as a Lean declaration -- it is documentation only.

title: Bounds on Maximum f(n)
content:
Comments document: f(n) >= 0.286 * n^2 and f(n) <= 0.446 * n^2, where f(n) = max_{pi} S(pi).

The gap [0.286, 0.446] shows the exact maximum is not yet known. NOTE: neither bound is formalized as a Lean declaration -- both are documentation only.
mathContext: These bounds from Konieczny (2015) leave room for improvement.
prerequisites: extremal maximum f(n) = max over pi of S(pi)
matching upper and lower bounds on n^2 coefficient
gap between known bounds as an open problem

title: Random Permutation Behavior
content:
A comment documents that for a random permutation,

S(pi) ~ (1 + e^-2)/4 * n^2 ~ 0.2838 * n^2

This shows most permutations violate the conjecture by the same amount as worst-case constructions! NOTE: this asymptotic is not formalized as a Lean declaration -- it is documentation only.
mathContext: e^-2 ~ 0.135, so (1 + e^-2)/4 ~ 0.2838. Almost identical to the lower bound 0.286.
prerequisites: expected value of S over random permutations

title: The Identity Permutation is Special
content:
A comment documents that S(iota) = o(n^2) for the identity permutation.

For iota(i) = i, consecutive sums are arithmetic progressions: sum_{i=u}^v i = (v-u+1)(u+v)/2.

The number of distinct such sums is O(n^1.5), not Theta(n^2).

This special case motivated Erdos's (false) conjecture. NOTE: this o(n^2) property is not formalized as a Lean declaration -- it is documentation only (the file defines identityPerm but proves no theorem about its S-value).
mathContext: Identity has fewer distinct sums because arithmetic progression sums have algebraic structure.
prerequisites: counting distinct sums of an arithmetic structure
O(n^1.5) growth for the identity permutation

title: Minimum Bounds g(n)
content:
A comment documents that g(n) >= c * n^(3/2) for some c > 0 (not formalized as a Lean declaration).

**MinimumConjecture** (a formal def in this file) asks: Is g(n) >= n^(2-o(1))? (conjectured, open)

where g(n) = min_{pi} S(pi).

Even the minimum is superlinear - every permutation has many distinct consecutive sums.
mathContext: The gap between n^1.5 (known) and n^(2-o(1)) (conjectured) is significant.
prerequisites: extremal minimum g(n) = min over pi of S(pi)
